title: Giving up the seat
hookLine: meditators were more likely to offer their seat to someone on crutches (Condon et al.)

cards: A waiting room. Three chairs against the wall. Two are taken by people scrolling their phones.
You take the third. A minute later the door opens and a woman comes in on crutches, wincing. There's nowhere for her to sit.
She leans against the wall with a small sigh. The two strangers don't look up. What happens next was the whole point of an experiment, though the person in the third chair had no idea.
The meditation course, the questionnaires: all of it was setup. This moment was the test.

teach.h: A COURSE, OR A WAITING LIST.
teach.b: First, the design. Psychologists Paul Condon, David DeSteno and their colleagues recruited adults for a meditation course.
Some took the course; others were put on a waiting list. Afterward, everyone was called back to the lab for what they thought was a test of thinking skills. Second, the staging.

The two people on their phones were actors, told to ignore the woman, and the woman on crutches was an actor too. The researchers wanted a hard case: when others are clearly doing nothing, it's easier to do nothing too.
Third, the result. The people who had meditated were noticeably more likely to stand up and offer her the seat than the people still on the waiting list.
Not everyone who meditated did it. But a sitting practice, done in a quiet room for weeks, showed up in a crowded one as someone getting out of a chair. Fourth, the old teachers.
In the Analects, a disciple named Fan Chi asks Confucius about ren, the Confucian virtue translated as benevolence or humaneness.

In James Legge's translation, the answer is just: "It is to love all men." Not a feeling to admire; a way of treating the person in front of you. Some readers find ren as much in small courtesies as in large deeds.
The test of a practice may not be how calm the sit felt. It may be a chair, an aching foot, and whether you notice them.

how: Some meditation teachers describe the real test of practice as how people treat others afterward; in Confucian teaching, ren (humaneness) is practiced through everyday courtesy toward the person in front of you.

games.q: what does “giving up the seat” mean?
o: quitting meditation to do more practical good
a custom of saving the best seat for a friend
meditators more often stood for a stranger in pain

games.q: inside the waiting room: tap the pairs.
p: more likely to offer the seat

s: the people in the study knew the waiting room was the real test
they thought they were there for a thinking test; the waiting room was staged.
everyone who meditated gave up the seat
not everyone did, but meditators were noticeably more likely to than people on the waiting list.
in the Analects, Legge has Confucius define ren as loving all men
asked about ren, the answer in Legge's translation is: it is to love all men.

games.q: you're in the third chair. the other two ignore the woman on crutches. what did the meditators tend to do?
o: follow the others and keep scrolling.
stand up and offer her the seat.
point her toward the front desk.
games.why: meditators were more likely to give up the seat, even while two strangers did nothing.

practice: Picture the places you'll be today, a bus, a line at the store, a parking lot, a meeting room, and in each one see a person who might need what you have: a seat, a place in line, the closer parking space, the chair nearest the door.
Choose one you could offer, then rest in the breath and let the choice wait for its moment.

wordCard.voice: Giving up the seat. In one experiment, people who had meditated were more likely to stand for a stranger on crutches, even while others ignored her. Today's word.

orig.note: ren: the Confucian virtue of humaneness or benevolence; Legge's Analects has Confucius define it as 'to love all men'.

carryVoice: Your line: the seat. The best offer is the one nobody has to ask for. Rest well.

sources.ref: Condon, Desbordes, Miller and DeSteno, "Meditation increases compassionate responses to suffering" (Psychological Science)

sources.q: It is to love all men.
